articles.title: How Milei Defused Argentina's Hyperinflation Bomb
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
Argentina was approaching monetary detonation. Its Treasury could not finance its deficits voluntarily, its central bank was effectively insolvent, and monthly inflation was accelerating above 12 percent.
That was just three years ago. Today, monthly inflation has fallen below 2 percent, sovereign spreads touched eight-year lows in July, and the central bank's gross reserves reached their highest level since 2019 in September. This is one of the most remarkable disinflations of the modern era to have occurred without dollarization, a currency board, or a new currency. Javier Milei did not merely slow the rate at which prices were rising; he dismantled the fiscal and monetary mechanism that was driving Argentina toward hyperinflation.
But as the events of late 2025 showed, that achievement remains vulnerable. A stabilization can be economically coherent and still be politically mortal. Argentina has restored a substantial degree of public sector solvency, but it has not yet made that solvency independent of the next election.
Deficits themselves do not make Argentina unique. What distinguished Argentina was how those deficits had to be financed. In a country with functioning capital markets and a credible government, the state sells bonds to domestic and foreign savers; it obtains command over present resources, while creditors receive claims on future tax revenues. Public borrowing may be undesirable or objectionable on other grounds, but so long as the government remains solvent in the long run, it is a financial operation that can be sustained over time without debt restructurings or bouts of high inflation.
Argentina had largely exhausted that option. After repeated inflationary crises and serial debt repudiations—nine sovereign defaults, most recently in 2020—investors would lend to the Treasury only at prohibitive rates. Borrowing at those rates would itself make the debt trajectory unsustainable, so creditors expected either another restructuring of dollar-denominated bonds or an inflationary liquidation of peso-denominated liabilities. Those expectations raised borrowing costs further, making the anticipated outcome more likely. The Argentine state had trapped itself in a doom loop.
So the government relied on the one creditor that couldn't refuse it: the central bank. Fiscal deficits were financed, directly or indirectly, by issuing pesos. But that brought it up against a second constraint. The inflationary effect of money creation depends not only on the quantity of money supplied but on the quantity people are willing to hold. And after decades of monetary abuse, Argentines wanted as few pesos as possible.
Every newly issued peso became a hot potato to be exchanged for goods, dollars, or inflation-protected assets. As the demand for real peso balances contracted, the government had to print ever larger quantities to extract the same real resources, which pushed prices up faster, which further reduced the willingness to hold pesos, which required still more issuance. That's the feedback loop of an economy approaching hyperinflation.
Rather than stop the process, the government tried to repress its visible symptoms—a task for which the country has a well-worn tool kit. Its most familiar instrument is the cepo cambiario, a web of capital and exchange controls with which the state prevents its citizens from freely satisfying their demand for dollars and hides the peso's depreciation behind an artificially strong official exchange rate. President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner imposed it in 2011; Mauricio Macri lifted it on taking the presidency, only to reinstate it amid the currency run of 2019; the leaders who followed tightened it further. Under the cepo, exchange rates multiplied. Exporters were forced to surrender their dollars below market value, while politically privileged importers bought them cheaply from the central bank. That arrangement punished exports, subsidized favored imports, invited corruption, and bled reserves.
The second instrument operated through the central bank's own balance sheet: extremely high nominal interest rates paid on short-term liabilities held mainly by commercial banks. These so-called remunerated liabilities were a standing bribe to the financial system to sit on its pesos rather than convert them into dollars or goods. Since those interest payments were themselves financed by creating new money for which there was no demand, they generated what Argentines call the quasi-fiscal deficit—a deficit produced not by the Treasury's spending programs but by the central bank's mounting interest bill. Paying interest to suppress monetary expansion today merely promised greater monetary expansion tomorrow.
By the end of 2023, the numbers had become grotesque. The Treasury's fiscal deficit stood at roughly 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), while the central bank's quasi-fiscal deficit approached 10 percent. Sovereign spreads hovered near 2,500 basis points—meaning that when an equivalent U.S. Treasury bond yielded 5 percent a year, Argentina would have had to pay around 30 percent to borrow in dollars. Monthly inflation hit 12.8 percent in November and was accelerating. (For perspective: Americans were furious when inflation peaked at 9 percent a year under President Joe Biden.) The gap between the official exchange rate and parallel rates exceeded 100 percent and at times approached 200 percent, strangling foreign trade. And the central bank's net international reserves stood at roughly negative $11 billion, the lowest level in its recorded history.
That was the machine Milei inherited on December 10, 2023: an insolvent Treasury, a central bank buried under remunerated liabilities, a rapidly contracting demand for the national currency, and a regulatory apparatus built to disguise the consequences of all three.
Argentina was not yet in hyperinflation. But it had entered its antechamber.
Milei's strategy was to restore the solvency of the Treasury and the central bank so that the controls concealing their insolvency could safely be removed. The sequencing was important. If he had scrapped every exchange control while the government still ran large deficits, the central bank still printed pesos to cover them, and net reserves were deeply negative, that could have accelerated rather than stopped a speculative run.
The first front was fiscal. Milei cut government spending, and not just in inflation-adjusted terms. Some cuts were explicit: Public works were halted, discretionary transfers to provincial governments were slashed, subsidies were pared back, and government employment contracted. (Such changes struck at many of the mechanisms through which Argentina's political class distributed patronage.) Other cuts operated through inflation itself: The government declined to fully index some nominal expenditures to rising prices, shrinking the real value of public salaries and pensions. This was socially painful, particularly for pensioners, but it allowed the fiscal correction to proceed faster than Congress would otherwise have permitted.
National primary spending fell by roughly a quarter in real terms in Milei's first year—an adjustment with few peacetime precedents—which brought national spending, as a share of the economy, back toward levels last seen in 2007–08. Within weeks of taking office, the government was posting monthly primary surpluses; it closed 2024 with a fiscal surplus and has treated balanced budgets as the nonnegotiable anchor ever since. That change altered the monetary regime before any formal institutional reform. Once the Treasury stopped requiring net financing from the central bank, the primary source of fiscally driven peso creation disappeared.
Milei also devalued the official exchange rate within days of taking office, bringing it closer to the market rate. That produced an immediate price shock, with monthly inflation exceeding 25 percent in December 2023. Critics called the devaluation inflationary, and in an immediate accounting sense, it was. But much of the inflation it unleashed was already latent, repressed behind an official exchange rate that almost nobody could access and nobody believed. By recognizing the accumulated depreciation at once, the government sharply narrowed the gap between official and parallel markets, restored exporters' incentives, and began dismantling expectations of an uncontrolled adjustment. After a transitional period, most exchange restrictions were lifted in April 2025.
Skeptics will note—correctly—that the liberalization co-incided with a new $20 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and will be tempted to conclude that it was this that made it possible to lift the cepo: just another bailout in a long history of Argentine bailouts. That reading misses the difference between financing a flow (the deficit) and refinancing a stock (the inherited debt).
Earlier IMF programs had poured external resources into governments that were still generating new fiscal imbalances, so the money flowed in while the pile of public liabilities kept growing—most spectacularly in 2018, when the largest loan in the IMF's history stabilized nothing. This time, the Treasury was already in surplus, and the facility operated on the stock inherited from the past: Argentina's largest external creditor was rolling over its own exposure, thickening the central bank's liquidity buffers, and stretching the horizon over which the old debt would be serviced. That support undoubtedly reinforced the program's healing dynamics and probably brought the lifting of the cepo forward. But it was neither a sufficient condition for success nor, over the medium term, a necessary one. A Treasury running surpluses and a central bank no longer bleeding pesos would eventually have rebuilt reserves and regained market access on their own, though this would have happened more slowly.
The second front was the central bank itself. Once the Treasury stopped demanding monetary financing, the Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) could sharply cut the interest rates paid on its remunerated liabilities. With lower expectations of inflation and depreciation, it was no longer necessary to pay enormous nominal rates to keep pesos from stampeding into goods and dollars.
The relationship ran in both directions. Falling inflation allowed lower nominal rates, lower rates shrank the central bank's interest bill, a smaller interest bill reduced future money creation, and reduced expected money creation further increased the demand for pesos. A virtuous circle began to replace the old doom loop.
The government then dismantled the central bank's stock of remunerated liabilities, shifting the job of absorbing excess pesos—and its cost—onto Treasury instruments. This did not make the debt disappear, but it lengthened maturities and placed the cost where it belonged: on the Treasury's accounts, under public and legislative scrutiny, rather than hidden within the central bank's balance sheet. The distinction matters. The quasi-fiscal deficit had allowed governments to claim more fiscal discipline than actually existed by parking part of the cost of stabilization outside the formal budget. Milei's consolidation made the state's liabilities transparent and stopped the central bank from autonomously compounding them through an escalating interest bill.
As confidence returned, sovereign spreads collapsed from roughly 2,500 basis points when Milei was elected to around 400 in July 2026, their lowest in eight years. That allowed the Treasury to roll over maturing debt at ever longer terms and lower cost. Argentina has not yet fully regained ordinary access to international capital markets; the government still leans on multilateral financing and domestic issuance to meet foreign-currency maturities, and spreads widened again, to above 600 by late September, as long-term U.S. rates rose and investors began to price the 2027 presidential election. But the probability of another restructuring has receded dramatically. The improvement shows on the central bank's balance sheet too: In 2026 alone, the BCRA has bought more than $14 billion in the foreign exchange market, and in early September gross reserves topped $50 billion, their highest level since 2019. Purchases have slowed sharply since the summer, and usable net reserves remain far smaller, but the direction of travel has reversed from the deeply negative position inherited in 2023.
All of this occurred alongside a modest but real reduction in taxes. The Impuesto PAIS, a major surcharge on foreign-currency transactions, was allowed to expire at the end of 2024. Export taxes were abolished for regional economies and thousands of industrial products and were cut for major agricultural exports on a declining schedule; tariffs, internal taxes on selected goods, and the wealth tax were also reduced, pushing the national tax burden to its lowest share of GDP in almost two decades. These cuts were modest relative to Milei's ambitions, but notable because they occurred without sacrificing the surplus. Milei did not balance the budget by raising taxes; he cut spending faster than revenue fell.
The macroeconomic result is hard to dispute. Monthly inflation, 25.5 percent in December 2023, was 1.7 percent in August 2026. Year-over-year inflation has fallen to 33.5 percent from 211 percent in 2023, and it is still declining.
Does all of this mean that Argentina is financially saved and that Milei has completed his task? No. The months before the October 2025 midterms show why.
When the opposition began climbing in the polls, and above all after it crushed the government's candidates in September's Buenos Aires provincial election, markets started pricing a scenario in which Milei lost the political capacity to defend his own agenda. The repricing was brutal. Country risk, which had been trading around 700 basis points in mid-August, doubled to nearly 1,500 by mid-September, and the peso depreciated by more than 20 percent over the episode, even though short-term interest rates soared and the authorities burned billions of scarce dollars trying to stabilize it.
Note what had not happened. The government had not abandoned the surplus, had not returned to monetary financing, and had not rebuilt the remunerated-liability machine. Milei's program had not secretly become insolvent; what triggered the crisis was the rising probability that its enemies might regain the power to make the state insolvent again. Nor was the panic irrational. Asset values depend on expected future policy, not just current policy. Savers who believe a future government will monetize deficits, impose controls, or restructure debt will sell pesos and Argentine bonds before that government takes office, and that means the anticipation of a regime reversal can generate, in advance, the very crisis the reversal would eventually have produced.
And this was not merely a panic among foreign fund managers. Ordinary Argentines know their political class too well and have learned to protect themselves by dollarizing; the threat of a fiscally irresponsible government had them fleeing the peso en masse. The central bank's statistics tell the story. Gross retail purchases of dollars reached some $5 billion in September and almost as much in October—double their previous monthly pace, and the heaviest retail dollarization since the eve of the election in 2019—before collapsing to barely a third of that rhythm the month after the vote.
The panic revealed a real weak point, though. Milei had fixed the flows but not yet the stocks: The state's liquid assets—its international reserves—still fell short of the bills coming due, whether pesos being dumped for dollars or hard-currency bonds maturing in the months ahead. Rebuilding a state's balance sheet takes years. Reserves accumulate purchase by purchase, and maturities lengthen only as fast as creditors' trust returns. Until that slow work is done, any rise in the perceived risk of a political reversal can abruptly close the state's access to refinancing, leaving it with maturing debts it cannot yet cover and a run on the peso it cannot stabilize with its own resources.
That was the gap the U.S. Treasury stepped in to fill. In October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent set up a $20 billion swap line with Argentina's central bank and—in an operation American taxpayers had every reason to question—bought pesos outright in the days before the vote. Bessent was bridging, for a few weeks, a gap that political panic had blown open. The intervention contained the panic just long enough for the election to remove its immediate political cause. On October 26, Milei's coalition took more than 40 percent of the vote, expanded its bloc in Congress, and locked in enough votes to sustain the president's vetoes. Within days, the peso steadied, spreads resumed their slide, and the central bank was buying dollars again. By year's end, Argentina had repaid the $2.5 billion it had actually drawn on the swap.
Still, the lesson is uncomfortable. A stabilization is consolidated only when an election can no longer plausibly revive expectations of default and monetary collapse. Argentina isn't there yet.
Time, if politics allows, will close the balance sheet gap. Reserves are being rebuilt, and maturities stretch a little further with every successful auction. But some of Milei's central libertarian promises are still, for now, only promises.
Milei inherited a country with no voluntary creditors, almost no demand for its currency, a Treasury hooked on monetary financing, a central bank trapped by its own interest bill, deeply negative net reserves, and capital controls that strangled trade while failing to stop depreciation. In less than three years, his government produced sustained fiscal surpluses, dismantled the quasi-fiscal time bomb, cut monthly inflation from 25 percent to below 2 percent, compressed sovereign spreads to eight-year lows, liberalized the exchange market, rebuilt reserves, and reduced taxes. And it did that without confiscating deposits, without a new default, and without raising the overall tax burden.
Hyperinflation is no natural disaster. It is the political consequence of a state that loses solvency and finances itself through a currency its citizens no longer wish to hold. Milei has stopped that process. Whether he has changed Argentina's institutions enough to prevent its return is a verdict that will arrive only after he leaves office.

articles.title: Court Allows Discovery as to Vindictive Prosecution Defense by Smartmatic's Parent Company
articles.content:
From U.S. v. SGO Corp. Ltd., decided Tuesday by Judge Kathleen Williams (S.D. Fla.):
For a six-year period, the Government investigated SGO executives for their role in a money laundering and bribery scheme related to the May, 2016 Philippine elections. The investigation culminated in a six-count indictment ("First Indictment"), returned on August 8, 2024, which charged [executives of] SGO and Smartmatic … [with] conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act ("FCPA") (Count I); violations of the FCPA (Count II); conspiracy to commit money laundering (Count III); and international laundering of monetary instruments (Counts IV, V, and VI). The FCPA "prohibits officers of a domestic concern from making corrupt payments to a 'foreign official.'"
SGO was not charged. In fact, SGO had been cooperating with the Government since 2021, years before the First Indictment was returned. {Although the Parties may dispute the breadth and quality of SGO's efforts to cooperate, there is no question that SGO and the Government were engaged in discussions and the exchange of documents related to this matter.}
The original trial date was set for October 7, 2024 … [but was eventually reset for 2026]….
As the court notes, the Trump Administration was skeptical of FCPA prosecutions, deprioritized FCPA enforcement generally, and "elected to close FCPA investigations into multiple companies." But despite that, in October 2025, the government added SGO as a defendant in the case. SGO then moved to dismiss the superseding indictment, alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, and sought discovery in support of that motion, "premised on political events that have embroiled Smartmatic in the wake of the 2020 election":
Since that election, multiple high-profile individuals and organizations connected to then-Former President Donald Trump have alleged that Smartmatic, a subsidiary of SGO, interfered in the election…. President Trump has also reposted content blaming Smartmatic for interfering in United States and Venezuelan elections, calling Smartmatic "disgraceful" and expressing that those who "rigged" the 2020 election must pay. In response to the statements by President Trump's confederates, Smartmatic brought various defamation suits, which are largely ongoing. SGO contends that President Trump's personal animus against SGO and assertion of its rights against President Trump's confederates precipitated the filing of the Superseding Indictment….
The court lays out the demanding standard for defendants' attempts to get discovery related to allegations of vindictive or selective prosecution, but concludes that in this case the standard was met. A brief excerpt (for more, including citations to precedents to which the court analogizes this case, see the full opinion):
First, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by evidence that the Government bucked a trend in enforcement activity in prosecuting the defendant…. [W]hile the Blanche and Bondi Memos and Executive Order 14209 explicitly announced an intention to rein in and limit FCPA enforcement, particularly against corporations, SGO was charged, nonetheless.
Second, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the timing between a defendant's assertion of a right and the allegedly vindictive prosecutorial act…. [Here,] it is telling that the Government chose not to indict SGO originally, that SGO was charged only after President Trump reassumed office and after SGO had been cooperating with the Government for years, and that the Government has presented no evidence adduced between the First and Superseding Indictments warranting SGO's addition as a defendant.
Third, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the Executive, prosecutor, or law enforcement's stated positions, even when they do not explicitly admit that the case was brought against the defendant for an improper purpose…. The Court finds probative not just that President Trump signed an executive order regarding FCPA enforcement but also that President Trump has personally expressed animus towards SGO regarding election interference. Indeed, President Trump's confederates were sued by SGO for making false claims regarding SGO's role in interfering with the 2020 presidential election that President Trump lost….
After evaluating the totality of the circumstances in this case, the Court has concluded that limited discovery regarding SGO's Motion to Dismiss is warranted…. [T]ere is "some evidence" tending to support SGO's Motion to Dismiss: the individual Defendants were charged over a year prior to when the Superseding Indictment against SGO was returned; for years prior to the initiation of this case and up until the Superseding Indictment was returned, SGO was cooperating with the Government; the Government charged SGO amidst a public shift away from charging defendants for similar FCPA violations; SGO brought suit against the President's confederates prior to being charged; and the President has expressed at least some degree of animus towards SGO. "It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here … to warrant the unusual step of … find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."
[T]he Government shall provide the Court with the following for ex parte and in camera review under seal:
- The prosecution memoranda regarding the initial indictment in this case and the subsequent Superseding Indictment of SGO;
- All communications, including emails, memoranda, and correspondence, between the Department of Justice—including principals and personnel in the Offices of the Attorney General, the Associate Attorney General, the Deputy Attorney General, and the Principal Deputy Attorney General—and former Acting United States Attorney Hayden O'Byrne, United States Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, and any member of the past and present prosecution team relating to or discussing the decision to charge SGO and when to charge SGO from January 1, 2025 to October 16, 2025; and
- Any emails sent by either former Acting United States Attorney Hayden O'Byrne or United States Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones to SGO's former and current counsel from January 1, 2025 to October 16, 2025.

articles.title: Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward
articles.content:
From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:
The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):
[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.
The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.
Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.
{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}
The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….
Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….
In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States, to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:
They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.
The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.
Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….
Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.
The post Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Arkansas Bar Official Allegedly Transferred Points from Some Bar Examinees to Others
articles.content:
From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday:
Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.
The full statement from the court:
An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.
As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.
Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.
* * * * *
In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.
Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.
Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.
Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.
The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.
The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.
As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.
* * * * *
We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.
